claim: T cell receptor (TCR) engagement opens Ca2+ release-activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channels.
source: T cell receptor (TCR) engagement opens Ca2+ release-activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channels and triggers formation of an immune synapse between T cells and antigen-presenting cells.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in T cell biology, supported by the broader scientific literature and the experimental context of the study.

claim: TCR engagement triggers formation of an immune synapse between T cells and antigen-presenting cells.
source: T cell receptor (TCR) engagement opens Ca2+ release-activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channels and triggers formation of an immune synapse between T cells and antigen-presenting cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge in immunology and forms the basis for the experimental system used in this study.

claim: At the synapse, actin reorganizes into a concentric lamellipod and lamella with retrograde actin flow.
source: At the synapse, actin reorganizes into a concentric lamellipod and lamella with retrograde actin flow that helps regulate the intensity and duration of TCR signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental observations presented in the manuscript, including imaging data showing actin organization.

claim: Retrograde actin flow helps regulate the intensity and duration of TCR signaling.
source: At the synapse, actin reorganizes into a concentric lamellipod and lamella with retrograde actin flow that helps regulate the intensity and duration of TCR signaling.
evidence: This is supported by prior literature and the experimental findings in this manuscript showing effects of actin dynamics on signaling.

claim: Ca2+ influx is required to drive actin organization and dynamics at the synapse.
source: We find that Ca2+ influx is required to drive actin organization and dynamics at the synapse.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing changes in actin organization upon Ca2+ removal.

claim: Calcium acts by promoting actin depolymerization.
source: Calcium acts by promoting actin depolymerization and localizing actin polymerization and the actin nucleation promotion factor WAVE2 to the periphery of the lamellipod while suppressing polymerization elsewhere.
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation experiments showing increased actin filament half-life when Ca2+ is removed.

claim: Calcium localizes actin polymerization to the periphery of the lamellipod.
source: Calcium acts by promoting actin depolymerization and localizing actin polymerization and the actin nucleation promotion factor WAVE2 to the periphery of the lamellipod while suppressing polymerization elsewhere.
evidence: This is demonstrated by photoactivation experiments showing selective incorporation of actin at the periphery in the presence of Ca2+.

claim: Calcium localizes the actin nucleation promotion factor WAVE2 to the periphery of the lamellipod.
source: Calcium acts by promoting actin depolymerization and localizing actin polymerization and the actin nucleation promotion factor WAVE2 to the periphery of the lamellipod while suppressing polymerization elsewhere.
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry and live-cell imaging of EGFP-Abi1 showing peripheral enrichment in the presence of Ca2+.

claim: Calcium suppresses actin polymerization elsewhere in the synapse outside the lamellipod periphery.
source: Calcium acts by promoting actin depolymerization and localizing actin polymerization and the actin nucleation promotion factor WAVE2 to the periphery of the lamellipod while suppressing polymerization elsewhere.
evidence: This is demonstrated by photoactivation experiments showing minimal actin incorporation in the lamella when Ca2+ is present.

claim: Ca2+-dependent retrograde actin flow corrals ER tubule extensions to the synapse center.
source: Ca2+-dependent retrograde actin flow corrals ER tubule extensions and STIM1/Orai1 complexes to the synapse center, creating a self-organizing process for CRAC channel localization.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing ER tubules moving centripetally with actin and accumulating in the ADZ.

claim: Ca2+-dependent retrograde actin flow corrals STIM1/Orai1 complexes to the synapse center.
source: Ca2+-dependent retrograde actin flow corrals ER tubule extensions and STIM1/Orai1 complexes to the synapse center, creating a self-organizing process for CRAC channel localization.
evidence: This is supported by imaging showing STIM1/Orai1 puncta moving centripetally with actin at similar velocities.

claim: Ca2+ influx creates a self-organizing process for CRAC channel localization.
source: Ca2+-dependent retrograde actin flow corrals ER tubule extensions and STIM1/Orai1 complexes to the synapse center, creating a self-organizing process for CRAC channel localization.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed effects of Ca2+ on actin flow and the resulting concentration of CRAC channels in the ADZ.

claim: Ca2+ is a critical regulator of actin organization and dynamics at the synapse.
source: Our results demonstrate a new role for Ca2+ as a critical regulator of actin organization and dynamics at the synapse, and reveal potential feedback loops through which Ca2+ influx may modulate TCR signaling.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experimental observations of Ca2+ effects on actin.

claim: Ca2+ influx may modulate TCR signaling through feedback loops.
source: Our results demonstrate a new role for Ca2+ as a critical regulator of actin organization and dynamics at the synapse, and reveal potential feedback loops through which Ca2+ influx may modulate TCR signaling.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed effects of Ca2+ on actin dynamics and the known role of actin in TCR signaling.

claim: Strong antigenic stimuli create three concentric regions at the immune synapse: a central supramolecular activation cluster (cSMAC), an intermediate zone (the peripheral SMAC, or pSMAC), and a zone at the synapse edge (the distal SMAC, or dSMAC).
source: Strong antigenic stimuli create three concentric regions (Monks et al., 1998; Grakoui et al., 1999): a central supramolecular activation cluster (cSMAC), an intermediate zone (the peripheral SMAC, or pSMAC), and a zone at the synapse edge (the distal SMAC, or dSMAC) (Freiberg et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by the cited references.

claim: TCRs assemble with scaffolding and signaling proteins to form microclusters in the dSMAC which migrate centripetally towards the cSMAC.
source: TCRs assemble with scaffolding and signaling proteins to form microclusters in the dSMAC which migrate centripetally towards the cSMAC (Grakoui et al., 1999; Krummel et al., 2000; Campi et al., 2005; Varma et al., 2006; Yokosuka et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: As TCR microclusters move, they activate a MAP kinase cascade and Ca2+ influx through CRAC channels.
source: As they move, TCR microclusters activate a MAP kinase cascade and Ca2+ influx through Ca2+ release-activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channels, both of which are essential to initiate gene expression programs that drive T cell proliferation and differentiation (Feske et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: MAP kinase cascade and Ca2+ influx through CRAC channels are essential to initiate gene expression programs that drive T cell proliferation and differentiation.
source: As they move, TCR microclusters activate a MAP kinase cascade and Ca2+ influx through Ca2+ release-activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channels, both of which are essential to initiate gene expression programs that drive T cell proliferation and differentiation (Feske et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Signaling by TCR microclusters is terminated as they enter the cSMAC by the dissociation of signaling proteins and endocytosis of TCRs.
source: Signaling by TCR microclusters is terminated as they enter the cSMAC by the dissociation of signaling proteins (Yokosuka et al., 2005; Campi et al., 2005; Varma et al., 2006) and endocytosis of TCRs (Lee et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2000; Das et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: The strength of signaling at the synapse reflects a dynamic balance between formation of new microclusters in the dSMAC/pSMAC and their disassembly and internalization in the cSMAC.
source: Thus, the strength of signaling at the synapse is thought to reflect a dynamic balance between formation of new microclusters in the dSMAC/pSMAC and their disassembly and internalization in the cSMAC.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the cited literature describing microcluster dynamics.

claim: Actin reorganization at the synapse is crucial for TCR microcluster assembly, movement and signaling.
source: Actin reorganization at the synapse is crucial for TCR microcluster assembly, movement and signaling (Babich et al., 2012; Campi et al., 2005; Delon et al., 1998; Kaizuka et al., 2007; Liu et al., 1995; Valitutti et al., 1995; Varma et al., 2006; Yi et al., 2012; Kumari et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: In the dSMAC, actin is dense and highly branched and exhibits rapid retrograde flow similar to actin in the lamellipod of migrating cells.
source: In the dSMAC, actin is dense and highly branched (Parsey and Lewis, 1993; Bunnell et al., 2001) and exhibits rapid retrograde flow similar to actin in the lamellipod of migrating cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: In the pSMAC region, actin is less dense and resembles a lamella with actin organized into concentric arcs by myosin IIA.
source: In the neighboring pSMAC region, actin is less dense and resembles a lamella with actin organized into concentric arcs by myosin IIA (Babich et al., 2012; Yi et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Actin is sparse in the actin-depleted zone (ADZ) corresponding to the cSMAC.
source: Actin is sparse in the actin-depleted zone (ADZ) corresponding to the cSMAC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about synapse structure.

claim: Centripetal actin flow transports TCR microclusters towards the cSMAC where they are disassembled, limiting the signaling lifetime of each microcluster to a few minutes.
source: First, it transports TCR microclusters towards the cSMAC where they are disassembled, limiting the signaling lifetime of each microcluster to a few minutes (Yu et al., 2010; Varma et al., 2006; Yokosuka et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Actin polymerization and depolymerization are critical for microcluster formation and function.
source: Second, actin polymerization and depolymerization are critical for microcluster formation and function, based on the ability of cytochalasin D (an actin polymerization inhibitor) and jasplakinolide (an actin depolymerization inhibitor) to rapidly quell microcluster formation, MAP kinase signaling, and Ca2+ influx at the synapse (Valitutti et al., 1995; Varma et al., 2006; Rivas et al., 2004; Babich et al., 2012; Yi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Cytochalasin D and jasplakinolide rapidly quell microcluster formation, MAP kinase signaling, and Ca2+ influx at the synapse.
source: Second, actin polymerization and depolymerization are critical for microcluster formation and function, based on the ability of cytochalasin D (an actin polymerization inhibitor) and jasplakinolide (an actin depolymerization inhibitor) to rapidly quell microcluster formation, MAP kinase signaling, and Ca2+ influx at the synapse (Valitutti et al., 1995; Varma et al., 2006; Rivas et al., 2004; Babich et al., 2012; Yi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: TCR stimulation drives actin reorganization by activating the Rho-family GTPases Rac1 and Cdc42.
source: TCR stimulation is known to drive actin reorganization by activating the Rho-family GTPases Rac1 and Cdc42, which function via Wiscott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASp) and WASp-family verprolin homologous protein (WAVE2) to initiate actin nucleation through the Arp2/3 complex (Billadeau et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Rac1 and Cdc42 function via WASp and WAVE2 to initiate actin nucleation through the Arp2/3 complex.
source: TCR stimulation is known to drive actin reorganization by activating the Rho-family GTPases Rac1 and Cdc42, which function via Wiscott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASp) and WASp-family verprolin homologous protein (WAVE2) to initiate actin nucleation through the Arp2/3 complex (Billadeau et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Actin polymerization collaborates with myosin IIA contractility to drive retrograde actin flow from the lamellipod to the ADZ.
source: Recent studies have shown that actin polymerization collaborates with myosin IIA contractility to drive retrograde actin flow from the lamellipod to the ADZ, although there is some disagreement as to their relative contributions (Babich et al., 2012; Yi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references, though the authors note some disagreement in the field.

claim: Elevated intracellular Ca2+ in T cells has been associated with motility arrest.
source: Elevated intracellular Ca2+ ([Ca2+]i) in T cells has been associated with such cytoskeleton-dependent processes as motility arrest (Negulescu et al., 1996; Bhakta et al., 2005), cell rounding (Donnadieu et al., 1994), cell spreading (Bunnell et al., 2001) and synapse stabilization (Negulescu et al., 1996; Krummel et al., 2000; Delon et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Elevated intracellular Ca2+ in T cells has been associated with cell rounding.
source: Elevated intracellular Ca2+ ([Ca2+]i) in T cells has been associated with such cytoskeleton-dependent processes as motility arrest (Negulescu et al., 1996; Bhakta et al., 2005), cell rounding (Donnadieu et al., 1994), cell spreading (Bunnell et al., 2001) and synapse stabilization (Negulescu et al., 1996; Krummel et al., 2000; Delon et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Elevated intracellular Ca2+ in T cells has been associated with cell spreading.
source: Elevated intracellular Ca2+ ([Ca2+]i) in T cells has been associated with such cytoskeleton-dependent processes as motility arrest (Negulescu et al., 1996; Bhakta et al., 2005), cell rounding (Donnadieu et al., 1994), cell spreading (Bunnell et al., 2001) and synapse stabilization (Negulescu et al., 1996; Krummel et al., 2000; Delon et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Elevated intracellular Ca2+ in T cells has been associated with synapse stabilization.
source: Elevated intracellular Ca2+ ([Ca2+]i) in T cells has been associated with such cytoskeleton-dependent processes as motility arrest (Negulescu et al., 1996; Bhakta et al., 2005), cell rounding (Donnadieu et al., 1994), cell spreading (Bunnell et al., 2001) and synapse stabilization (Negulescu et al., 1996; Krummel et al., 2000; Delon et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: T cells express a range of Ca2+-sensitive proteins known to regulate actin depolymerization, severing, bundling, and capping.
source: In addition, T cells express a range of Ca2+-sensitive proteins known to regulate actin depolymerization, severing, bundling, and capping (Babich and Burkhardt, 2013; Joseph et al., 2014; Janmey, 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: TCR engagement elicits Ca2+ influx through CRAC channels via a cascade in which PLCγ generates IP3, releasing Ca2+ from the ER and causing STIM1 to redistribute to ER-PM junctions where it traps and activates Orai1.
source: TCR engagement is known to elicit Ca2+ influx through CRAC channels via a cascade in which PLCγ generates inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3), releasing Ca2+ from the ER and causing the ER Ca2+ sensor STIM1 to redistribute to ER-plasma membrane (PM) junctions (Wu et al., 2006; Luik et al., 2006) where it traps and activates Orai1, the pore-forming subunit of the CRAC channel (Luik et al., 2006; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: STIM1 and Orai1 colocalize at early times at the immune synapse and later at the distal pole of the cell.
source: STIM1 and Orai1 colocalize at early times at the immune synapse (Lioudyno et al., 2008; Barr et al., 2008) and later at the distal pole of the cell (Barr et al., 2008), but functional CRAC channel complexes as indicated by Ca2+ influx have only been shown at the synaptic contact zone (Lioudyno et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Functional CRAC channel complexes as indicated by Ca2+ influx have only been shown at the synaptic contact zone.
source: STIM1 and Orai1 colocalize at early times at the immune synapse (Lioudyno et al., 2008; Barr et al., 2008) and later at the distal pole of the cell (Barr et al., 2008), but functional CRAC channel complexes as indicated by Ca2+ influx have only been shown at the synaptic contact zone (Lioudyno et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: After settling on stimulatory coverslips, cells spread over several minutes until they reached a constant size and roughly circular shape.
source: After settling on stimulatory coverslips, cells spread over several minutes until they reached a constant size and roughly circular shape.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Puncta containing STIM1 and Orai1 appeared at the contact zone beginning within seconds of initial contact and continuing through the spreading phase.
source: Puncta containing STIM1 and Orai1 appeared at the contact zone beginning within seconds of initial contact and continuing through the spreading phase.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: After cells had spread fully, colocalized puncta of STIM1 and Orai1 continued to increase in number and intensity over the next several minutes and appeared to be confined to the center of the synapse in 68 of 82 cells.
source: After cells had spread fully (3–7 min after contact with the coverslip), colocalized puncta of STIM1 and Orai1 continued to increase in number and intensity over the next several minutes and appeared to be confined to the center of the synapse (68 of 82 cells; Figure 1A and Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments, with quantification provided.

claim: In a minority of cells (27 of 68 cells), puncta containing STIM1 and Orai1 were detected near the periphery and moved toward the center of the synapse.
source: In a minority of cells (27 of 68 cells), puncta containing STIM1 and Orai1 were detected near the periphery and moved toward the center of the synapse (Figure 1B,C, Video 1) with an average velocity of 47 ± 3 nm/s (n = 24 puncta; mean ± SEM).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments, with quantification provided.

claim: STIM1/Orai1 puncta moved toward the center of the synapse with an average velocity of 47 ± 3 nm/s (n = 24 puncta; mean ± SEM).
source: In a minority of cells (27 of 68 cells), puncta containing STIM1 and Orai1 were detected near the periphery and moved toward the center of the synapse (Figure 1B,C, Video 1) with an average velocity of 47 ± 3 nm/s (n = 24 puncta; mean ± SEM).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the imaging experiments.

claim: Motile STIM1/Orai1 puncta were more frequently detected in 0.5–0.8 mM extracellular Ca2+ (48% of 33 cells) than in 2 mM Ca2+o (31% of 35 cells).
source: These motile puncta were more frequently detected in 0.5–0.8 mM extracellular Ca2+ (Ca2+o; 48% of 33 cells) than in 2 mM Ca2+o(31% of 35 cells), probably because a greater degree of ER Ca2+ depletion is expected under the reduced [Ca2+]o conditions.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: Puncta of colocalized STIM1 and Orai1 correspond to ER-PM junctions where STIM1-bound Orai1 conducts Ca2+ into the cell.
source: Puncta of colocalized STIM1 and Orai1 correspond to ER-PM junctions where STIM1-bound Orai1 conducts Ca2+ into the cell (Luik et al., 2006; Wu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: As the synapse matures, ER-PM junctions become concentrated in the center of the contact zone.
source: Thus, our results suggest that as the synapse matures ER-PM junctions become concentrated in the center of the contact zone, and individual ER-PM junctions loaded with STIM1 and Orai1 translocate from the periphery to further increase the density of Ca2+ influx sites in the center.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the imaging data showing STIM1/Orai1 accumulation in the center.

claim: Individual ER-PM junctions loaded with STIM1 and Orai1 translocate from the periphery to increase the density of Ca2+ influx sites in the center.
source: Thus, our results suggest that as the synapse matures ER-PM junctions become concentrated in the center of the contact zone, and individual ER-PM junctions loaded with STIM1 and Orai1 translocate from the periphery to further increase the density of Ca2+ influx sites in the center.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation of motile STIM1/Orai1 puncta.

claim: Cells formed a peripheral lamellipod characterized by a bright band of actin that appeared striated and ruffled in and out of the TIRF plane.
source: In agreement with previous reports (Bunnell et al., 2001; Kaizuka et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2010; Babich et al., 2012; Yi et al., 2012), cells formed a peripheral lamellipod characterized by a bright band of actin that appeared striated and ruffled in and out of the TIRF plane.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments, consistent with prior literature.

claim: At the inner edge of the lamellipod, actin density dropped off sharply, marking the transition into the lamella region where actin formed arc-like structures encircling a central ADZ.
source: At the inner edge of the lamellipod, actin density dropped off sharply, marking the transition into the lamella region where actin formed arc-like structures encircling a central ADZ (Video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Actin moved continually in a radial retrograde direction at velocities that declined from ~100 nm/s at the cell edge to near 0 nm/s at the border of the ADZ.
source: Actin moved continually in a radial retrograde direction at velocities that declined from ~100 nm/s at the cell edge to near 0 nm/s at the border of the ADZ (data not shown).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: The highest density of STIM1 puncta occurred within the ADZ while dimmer, more dynamic STIM1-containing tubules extended into the lamella in 21 of 21 cells.
source: The highest density of STIM1 puncta occurred within the ADZ while dimmer, more dynamic STIM1-containing tubules extended into the lamella (21 of 21 cells; Figure 1D and Video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: STIM1 puncta in the lamella move centripetally with and at the same velocity as F-actin.
source: Kymograph analysis shows that STIM1 puncta in the lamella move centripetally with and at the same velocity as F-actin (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by kymograph analysis in the manuscript.

claim: The advancing actin cytoskeletal network moves STIM1/Orai1 puncta and the associated ER-PM junctions towards the ADZ.
source: These observations suggest that the advancing actin cytoskeletal network moves STIM1/Orai1 puncta and the associated ER-PM junctions towards the ADZ.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that STIM1 and actin move together at the same velocity.

claim: The ER appeared in the TIRF evanescent field within minutes of cell contact with the stimulatory coverslips and expanded peripherally as cells spread.
source: The ER appeared in the TIRF evanescent field within minutes of cell contact with the stimulatory coverslips and expanded peripherally as cells spread (Figure 2A and Video 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: The ER near the PM was highly enriched in the ADZ in 20 of 20 cells in both tubular and sheet-like structures.
source: The ER near the PM was highly enriched in the ADZ (20 of 20 cells) in both tubular and sheet-like structures that became more centrally concentrated and immobile as the ring of actin surrounding the ADZ contracted.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Dynamic ER tubules extended from the ADZ toward the lamellipod in 16 of 20 cells.
source: Dynamic ER tubules extended from the ADZ toward the lamellipod (16 of 20 cells; Figure 2B, pink arrows) and occasionally traversed the lamella/lamellipod border, then either rapidly retracted along a similar trajectory (10 of 20 cells; Figure 2Bii, green arrows), or appeared to bend before moving centripetally (20 of 20 cells; Figure 2Biii, cyan arrows).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: A subset of ER tubules that penetrated the lamellipod remained relatively immobile in actin-sparse regions in 8 of 20 cells.
source: A subset of tubules that penetrated the lamellipod remained relatively immobile in actin-sparse regions (8 of 20 cells; Figure 2Biii, yellow arrows).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: ER tubules can extend by sliding along the sides of microtubules or by attaching to the tips of growing microtubules.
source: In general, ER tubules can extend by sliding along the sides of microtubules or by attaching to the tips of growing microtubules (Waterman-Storer and Salmon, 1998) through an interaction between STIM1 and the microtubule tip attachment proteins EB1 and EB3 (Grigoriev et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: STIM1 interacts with the microtubule tip attachment proteins EB1 and EB3.
source: In general, ER tubules can extend by sliding along the sides of microtubules or by attaching to the tips of growing microtubules (Waterman-Storer and Salmon, 1998) through an interaction between STIM1 and the microtubule tip attachment proteins EB1 and EB3 (Grigoriev et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: EB1 was seen at the tips of many extending ER tubules.
source: In Jurkat cells expressing EB1 labeled with EGFP (EB1-EGFP) and ER-mCh, EB1 was seen at the tips of many extending ER tubules (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Video 4), confirming that ER tubules can extend toward the synapse periphery by attaching to the tips of growing microtubules.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: ER tubules can extend toward the synapse periphery by attaching to the tips of growing microtubules.
source: In Jurkat cells expressing EB1 labeled with EGFP (EB1-EGFP) and ER-mCh, EB1 was seen at the tips of many extending ER tubules (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Video 4), confirming that ER tubules can extend toward the synapse periphery by attaching to the tips of growing microtubules.
evidence: This is confirmed by the observation of EB1 at ER tubule tips.

claim: ER tubules rarely extended into the lamellipod, likely reflecting infrequent microtubule forays into the lamellipod.
source: ER tubules rarely extended into the lamellipod, likely reflecting infrequent microtubule forays into the lamellipod (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Video 5), as has been reported for migrating epithelial cells (Waterman-Storer and Salmon, 1997).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments, with an interpretation based on microtubule behavior.

claim: At the lamellipod/lamella border, the majority of EB1 reoriented and moved parallel to the synapse edge or disappeared as they moved above the TIRF evanescent field.
source: Like ER tubules, EB1 moved roughly radially though the ADZ and lamella, but at the lamellipod/lamella border the majority reoriented and moved parallel to the synapse edge or disappeared as they moved above the TIRF evanescent field (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Video 5).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: ER tubules infrequently enter the lamellipod because microtubules cannot easily penetrate this thin, actin-dense compartment.
source: These findings suggest that ER tubules infrequently enter the lamellipod because microtubules cannot easily penetrate this thin, actin-dense compartment.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observations of ER and microtubule behavior.

claim: ER tubules undergoing retrograde movement in the lamella were commonly sandwiched between actin arcs in 17 of 20 cells.
source: ER tubules undergoing retrograde movement in the lamella were commonly sandwiched between actin arcs (17 of 20 cells; Figure 2Biii, cyan arrows, and Video 3), and both moved at the same velocity (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: ER tubules and actin arcs moved at the same velocity.
source: ER tubules undergoing retrograde movement in the lamella were commonly sandwiched between actin arcs (17 of 20 cells; Figure 2Biii, cyan arrows, and Video 3), and both moved at the same velocity (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by kymograph analysis.

claim: The similar retrograde velocities of isolated STIM1/Orai1 puncta (47 ± 3 nm/s) and lamellar actin (36 ± 6 nm/s) suggest that retrograde actin flow sweeps ER-PM junctions into the ADZ.
source: Moreover, the similar retrograde velocities of isolated STIM1/Orai1 puncta (47 ± 3 nm/s, mean ± SEM, n = 24 particles; Figure 1C) and lamellar actin (36 ± 6 nm/s, mean ± SEM, n = 18 cells; Figure 6F) suggest that retrograde actin flow also sweeps ER-PM junctions into the ADZ.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the similar velocities measured in the experiments.

claim: The ER at the synapse is dynamic, with peripheral extension on microtubules continually balanced by retraction imposed by retrograde actin flow.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that the ER at the synapse is dynamic, with peripheral extension on microtubules continually balanced by retraction imposed by retrograde actin flow.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observations of ER dynamics in relation to microtubules and actin.

claim: In the presence of Ca2+o, cells formed a clearly defined lamellipod and lamella with extensive ruffling of the lamellipod and continuous bulk retrograde actin flow.
source: In the presence of Ca2+o, cells formed a clearly defined lamellipod and lamella (Figure 3A, left) with extensive ruffling of the lamellipod and continuous bulk retrograde actin flow as described above in cells expressing GFP-actin (Video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Perfusion with Ca2+-free medium caused several rapid and profound changes in the organization and dynamics of F-tractin-P at the synapse in the majority of cells (38 of 45).
source: Perfusion with Ca2+-free medium to terminate Ca2+ influx through CRAC channels caused several rapid and profound changes in the organization and dynamics of F-tractin-P at the synapse. In the majority of cells (38 of 45), the distinguishing features of the lamellipod and lamella were lost: ruffling at the periphery was greatly reduced and lamella actin arcs became less apparent, the lamella/lamellipod boundary disappeared as F-actin became more uniformly distributed across the synapse, and in some cells (15 of 45) F-actin extended into the ADZ (Figure 3A and Video 6).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Ca2+o removal greatly reduced ruffling at the periphery and made lamella actin arcs less apparent.
source: In the majority of cells (38 of 45), the distinguishing features of the lamellipod and lamella were lost: ruffling at the periphery was greatly reduced and lamella actin arcs became less apparent, the lamella/lamellipod boundary disappeared as F-actin became more uniformly distributed across the synapse, and in some cells (15 of 45) F-actin extended into the ADZ (Figure 3A and Video 6).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Ca2+o removal caused the lamella/lamellipod boundary to disappear as F-actin became more uniformly distributed across the synapse.
source: In the majority of cells (38 of 45), the distinguishing features of the lamellipod and lamella were lost: ruffling at the periphery was greatly reduced and lamella actin arcs became less apparent, the lamella/lamellipod boundary disappeared as F-actin became more uniformly distributed across the synapse, and in some cells (15 of 45) F-actin extended into the ADZ (Figure 3A and Video 6).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: In some cells (15 of 45), F-actin extended into the ADZ upon Ca2+o removal.
source: In the majority of cells (38 of 45), the distinguishing features of the lamellipod and lamella were lost: ruffling at the periphery was greatly reduced and lamella actin arcs became less apparent, the lamella/lamellipod boundary disappeared as F-actin became more uniformly distributed across the synapse, and in some cells (15 of 45) F-actin extended into the ADZ (Figure 3A and Video 6).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Ca2+o removal severely reduced the centripetal movement of actin and any remaining movement was less radial and more randomly oriented.
source: Most strikingly, the centripetal movement of actin was severely reduced and any remaining movement was less radial and more randomly oriented (Figure 3B and Video 6).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments using STICS analysis.

claim: The effects of Ca2+o removal on actin all reversed within seconds of restoring Ca2+o.
source: These effects all reversed within seconds of restoring Ca2+o, and were also observed in cells expressing GFP-actin (data not shown).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CRAC channel function with 2-APB in the presence of Ca2+o produced a similar response to Ca2+o removal in 11 of 14 cells.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of CRAC channel function with 2-aminoethyldiphenyl borate (2-APB) in the presence of Ca2+o produced a similar response (11 of 14 cells; Figure 3C,D), indicating that changes in actin organization and dynamics result from the inhibition of Ca2+ influx through CRAC channels rather than from the removal of Ca2+o itself.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Changes in actin organization and dynamics result from the inhibition of Ca2+ influx through CRAC channels rather than from the removal of Ca2+o itself.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of CRAC channel function with 2-aminoethyldiphenyl borate (2-APB) in the presence of Ca2+o produced a similar response (11 of 14 cells; Figure 3C,D), indicating that changes in actin organization and dynamics result from the inhibition of Ca2+ influx through CRAC channels rather than from the removal of Ca2+o itself.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the similar effects of 2-APB and Ca2+o removal.

claim: In primary human T lymphoblasts, Ca2+o removal altered the distribution of synaptic actin and reduced ruffling and retrograde flow in 20 of 21 cells.
source: T lymphoblasts plated on anti-CD3- and ICAM-1-coated coverslips formed a distinct lamellipod with rapid retrograde actin flow as described previously (Comrie et al., 2015) and Ca2+ removal altered the distribution of synaptic actin and reduced ruffling and retrograde flow (20 of 21 cells; Figure 3E, Video 7).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments with primary T cells.

claim: Ca2+ removal slowed actin flow by 44% on average in primary T lymphoblasts, and Ca2+o reperfusion restored it to 97% of the initial velocity.
source: Kymograph analysis showed that on average, Ca2+ removal slowed actin flow by 44% and Ca2+o reperfusion restored it to 97% of the initial velocity (Figure 3F, Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the imaging experiments.

claim: Ca2+o removal narrowed the lamellipod by 61% in primary T lymphoblasts, while Ca2+o restoration returned the lamellipod to 82% of its initial width.
source: Ca2+o removal narrowed the lamellipod by 61%, while Ca2+o restoration returned the lamellipod to 82% of its initial width (Figure 3E, Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the imaging experiments.

claim: Primary T lymphoblasts and Jurkat T cells responded similarly to changes in Ca2+o.
source: Thus, primary T lymphoblasts and Jurkat T cells responded similarly to changes in Ca2+o, supporting the use of Jurkat T cells as a physiologically relevant model system for studying the effects of Ca2+ on actin dynamics at the synapse.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of experimental results from both cell types.

claim: In the absence of Ca2+o, very few ER tubules were visible in the lamella/lamellipod region by TIRF although small segments of ER were seen near the cell edge.
source: In the absence of Ca2+o, very few ER tubules were visible in the lamella/lamellipod region by TIRF although small segments of ER were seen near the cell edge, suggesting that under these conditions, peripheral ER tubules extend in the Z dimension out of the TIRF evanescent field (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Readdition of Ca2+o initiated a rapid increase in the density of ER tubules in the lamella consistent with their reentry into the evanescent field, and tubules moved centripetally as retrograde actin flow resumed in 6 of 6 cells.
source: Readdition of Ca2+o initiated a rapid increase in the density of ER tubules in the lamella consistent with their reentry into the evanescent field, and tubules moved centripetally as retrograde actin flow resumed (6 of 6 cells; Figure 4B,C, and Video 9).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Ca2+ influx through CRAC channels helps to corral extended peripheral ER tubules back to the center of the synapse by promoting retrograde actin flow.
source: These results demonstrate that Ca2+ influx through CRAC channels helps to corral extended peripheral ER tubules back to the center of the synapse by promoting retrograde actin flow.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observations of ER dynamics in response to Ca2+ manipulations.

claim: Blocking Ca2+ influx increased F-tractin-P fluorescence intensity (and thus F-actin density) by 20–30%.
source: One clue to the mechanism of calcium's effects on actin dynamics at the synapse was that blocking Ca2+ influx increased F-tractin-P fluorescence intensity (and thus F-actin density) by 20–30% (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Ca2+o removal increased the F-tractin-P fluorescence at the synapse when viewed by spinning disk confocal microscopy.
source: Elevated F-tractin-P fluorescence did not appear to be a consequence of bulk movement of cellular structures into the evanescent field (such as might result from changes in cell shape) because Ca2+o removal also increased the F-tractin-P fluorescence at the synapse when viewed by spinning disk confocal microscopy, which samples a much thicker optical section (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments using a different imaging modality.

claim: The decline in [Ca2+]i following Ca2+o removal was closely followed by an increase in F-tractin-P fluorescence that plateaued ~30 s after [Ca2+]i.
source: The decline in [Ca2+]i was closely followed by an increase in F-tractin-P fluorescence that plateaued ~30 s after [Ca2+]i (Figure 5B, right).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the simultaneous Ca2+ and actin imaging experiments.

claim: Readdition of Ca2+o caused [Ca2+]i to rise and F-actin to decline, demonstrating a rapidly reversible effect on F-actin density.
source: Similarly, readdition of Ca2+o caused [Ca2+]i to rise and F-actin to decline, demonstrating a rapidly reversible effect on F-actin density.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the simultaneous Ca2+ and actin imaging experiments.

claim: The level of F-actin declined as [Ca2+]i increased, and this relationship was similar regardless of whether measurements were made before or after Ca2+ removal.
source: In this group of 26 cells the level of F-actin declined as [Ca2+]i increased, and this relationship was similar regardless of whether measurements were made before or after Ca2+ removal.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments correlating Ca2+ and F-actin levels.

claim: The level of F-actin was highly correlated with [Ca2+]i (R2 = 0.83) but not with [Ca2+]o (R2 = 0.22).
source: The level of F-actin was highly correlated with [Ca2+]i (R2 = 0.83) but not with [Ca2+]o (R2 = 0.22), and 2-APB application and Ca2+o removal had similar effects on F-tractin-P density, demonstrating that intracellular Ca2+ reversibly regulates the density of F-actin at the synapse.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the correlation between Ca2+ and F-actin levels.

claim: Intracellular Ca2+ reversibly regulates the density of F-actin at the synapse.
source: The level of F-actin was highly correlated with [Ca2+]i (R2 = 0.83) but not with [Ca2+]o (R2 = 0.22), and 2-APB application and Ca2+o removal had similar effects on F-tractin-P density, demonstrating that intracellular Ca2+ reversibly regulates the density of F-actin at the synapse.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation analysis and the effects of Ca2+ manipulations.

claim: With Ca2+o present, photoactivated actin moved toward the center of the synapse at velocities comparable to those previously reported from kymograph measurements, and moved faster in the lamellipod than in the lamella.
source: With Ca2+o present, photoactivated actin moved toward the center of the synapse at velocities comparable to those previously reported from kymograph measurements (Yi et al., 2012; Babich et al., 2012), and moved faster in the lamellipod than in the lamella as expected (Figure 6B, C, F and Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the photoactivation experiments, consistent with prior literature.

claim: In the absence of Ca2+o, mean actin velocity decreased by 41% in the region of the lamellipod and by 64% in the lamella.
source: In the absence of Ca2+o, mean actin velocity decreased by 41% in the region of the lamellipod and by 64% in the lamella (Figure 6B, C, F and Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the photoactivation experiments.

claim: Ca2+ removal extended the mean actin filament half-life by 17% in the lamella and 23% in the lamellipod region.
source: The decay kinetics in 2 mM Ca2+o were similar in the lamella and lamellipod, and Ca2+ removal extended the mean actin filament half-life by 17% in the lamella and 23% in the lamellipod region (Figure 6G and Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the photoactivation experiments.

claim: Ca2+ influx accelerates actin depolymerization at the synapse.
source: Thus, our findings indicate that Ca2+ influx accelerates actin depolymerization at the synapse.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the photoactivation experiments showing increased actin filament half-life when Ca2+ is removed.

claim: After inhibition of myosin ATPase activity with blebbistatin, Ca2+o removal induced a 30% increase in F-actin density, similar to its effect in the absence of the drug.
source: However, after inhibition of myosin ATPase activity with blebbistatin, Ca2+o removal induced a 30% increase in F-actin density (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B), similar to its effect in the absence of the drug (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with blebbistatin.

claim: Ca2+ regulates F-actin density and depolymerization at the synapse independently of myosin.
source: These results suggest that Ca2+ regulates F-actin density and depolymerization at the synapse independently of myosin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that blebbistatin does not prevent Ca2+ effects on F-actin.

claim: In the absence of Ca2+o, GFP fluorescence increased immediately in the ADZ upon photoactivation, followed by a slower rise throughout the lamella as fluorescent actin monomers diffused through the cytosol and incorporated into F-actin.
source: In the absence of Ca2+o, GFP fluorescence increased immediately in the ADZ upon photoactivation, followed by a slower rise throughout the lamella as fluorescent actin monomers diffused through the cytosol and incorporated into F-actin.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the photoactivation experiments.

claim: In the absence of Ca2+o, the fluorescence rise reached the cell's edge within 3 s of photoactivation and covered most of the actin-rich area of the synapse, reflecting widespread polymerization.
source: The fluorescence rise reached the cell's edge within 3 s of photoactivation, consistent with the rapid diffusion of monomeric actin in cells, and covered most of the actin-rich area of the synapse, reflecting widespread polymerization (Figure 7A,C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the photoactivation experiments.

claim: In the presence of Ca2+o, within 2 s of photoactivation in the ADZ, fluorescence increased selectively in a narrow band around the periphery of the lamellipod.
source: In the presence of Ca2+o, actin polymerization was strikingly different. Within 2 s of photoactivation in the ADZ, fluorescence increased selectively in a narrow band around the periphery of the lamellipod (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the photoactivation experiments.

claim: In the presence of Ca2+o, fluorescence at the periphery peaked within ~6 s, then declined slightly as the combination of peripheral incorporation and centripetal flow labeled the entire lamellipod.
source: Fluorescence at the periphery peaked within ~6 s, then declined slightly as the combination of peripheral incorporation and centripetal flow labeled the entire lamellipod, generating a wide band of fluorescent actin that dropped off sharply at the lamella/lamellipod border (Figure 7B,D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the photoactivation experiments.

claim: In the presence of Ca2+o, fluorescence in the lamella increased only minimally during the 30 s following photoactivation.
source: In contrast, fluorescence in the lamella increased only minimally during the 30 s following photoactivation.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the photoactivation experiments.

claim: Ca2+ influx effectively promotes actin polymerization at the distal edge of the lamellipod while suppressing polymerization elsewhere throughout the synapse.
source: These results demonstrate that Ca2+ influx effectively promotes actin polymerization at the distal edge of the lamellipod while suppressing polymerization elsewhere throughout the synapse.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the photoactivation experiments showing selective actin incorporation at the periphery.

claim: Ca2+o enriched the level of endogenous WAVE2 at the synapse periphery.
source: Using immunocytochemistry we found that Ca2+o enriched the level of endogenous WAVE2 at the synapse periphery (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunocytochemistry experiments.

claim: Abi1 was highly enriched at the synapse periphery in the presence of Ca2+o.
source: Abi1 was highly enriched at the synapse periphery in the presence of Ca2+o as expected (Video 12, Figure 7G, left, right panels), and Ca2+o removal caused Abi1 to become diffusely distributed throughout the synapse in a reversible manner (Figure 7G, middle, Figure 7H,I).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the live-cell imaging experiments.

claim: Ca2+o removal caused Abi1 to become diffusely distributed throughout the synapse in a reversible manner.
source: Abi1 was highly enriched at the synapse periphery in the presence of Ca2+o as expected (Video 12, Figure 7G, left, right panels), and Ca2+o removal caused Abi1 to become diffusely distributed throughout the synapse in a reversible manner (Figure 7G, middle, Figure 7H,I).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the live-cell imaging experiments.

claim: Ca2+ restricts actin polymerization to the lamellipod edge at least in part through controlling the location of nucleation.
source: The finding that Ca2+ localizes the WAVE2 complex to the lamellipod edge suggests that Ca2+ restricts actin polymerization to the synapse periphery at least in part through controlling the location of nucleation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that Ca2+ localizes WAVE2/Abi1 to the periphery.

claim: Ca2+ acts at multiple levels to organize actin and promote retrograde flow.
source: We found that Ca2+ influx through CRAC channels acts at multiple levels to organize actin and promote retrograde flow, which in turn drives ER remodeling and the localization of STIM1 and Orai1 to the center of the synapse.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental findings in the study.

claim: Ca2+ influx drives ER remodeling and the localization of STIM1 and Orai1 to the center of the synapse through its action on actin.
source: We found that Ca2+ influx through CRAC channels acts at multiple levels to organize actin and promote retrograde flow, which in turn drives ER remodeling and the localization of STIM1 and Orai1 to the center of the synapse.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings showing Ca2+ effects on actin and ER dynamics.

claim: Ca2+ self-organizes CRAC channels at the synapse while creating feedback loops that may help regulate T cell sensitivity to antigen.
source: In this way, Ca2+ self-organizes CRAC channels at the synapse while creating feedback loops that may help regulate T cell sensitivity to antigen.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed self-organizing effects of Ca2+ on CRAC channel localization.

claim: Bunnell et al demonstrated that intracellular Ca2+ is required for actin accumulation and cell spreading during the early phase of synapse formation.
source: In a pioneering study, Bunnell et al demonstrated that intracellular Ca2+ is required for actin accumulation and cell spreading during the early phase of synapse formation; however, the failure of the cells to spread in the absence of Ca2+o precluded study of calcium's effects on the mature synapse (Bunnell et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a summary of prior work from the cited reference.

claim: Ca2+ acts in two ways to spatially restrict actin polymerization at the mature synapse: by promoting polymerization around the cell perimeter and by suppressing polymerization throughout the rest of the contact area.
source: Calcium acts in two ways to spatially restrict actin polymerization at the mature synapse: by promoting polymerization around the cell perimeter and by suppressing polymerization throughout the rest of the contact area.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the photoactivation experiments.

claim: The extensive polymerization at the lamellipod edge is closely paralleled by the recruitment of the WAVE2/Abi1 complex to the periphery.
source: The extensive polymerization at the lamellipod edge is closely paralleled by the recruitment of the WAVE2/Abi1 complex to the periphery (Figure 7), where it presumably activates Arp2/3 to initiate actin polymerization and branching (Takenawa and Suetsugu, 2007).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments showing correlation between polymerization and WAVE2/Abi1 localization.

claim: Ca2+ may direct WAVE2/Abi1 to the periphery by stimulating PI3K localization to the lamellipod, where generation of PIP3 may recruit the WAVE2 complex to the membrane.
source: One possible mechanism is suggested by the ability of Ca2+ to stimulate PI3K localization to the lamellipod of migrating cells, where generation of phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3) may recruit the WAVE2 complex to the membrane (Oikawa et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism based on prior literature about Ca2+ effects in other cell types.

claim: Ca2+ may exert additional effects through its ability to promote GTP loading of Rac, a GTPase essential for WAVE2-mediated actin nucleation.
source: Ca2+ may exert additional effects through its ability to promote GTP loading of Rac, a GTPase essential for WAVE2-mediated actin nucleation (Fleming et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism based on prior literature.

claim: Ca2+-sensitive capping proteins expressed in T cells such as gelsolin or CapG are attractive candidates for suppressing polymerization elsewhere in the lamella and lamellipod.
source: The mechanism by which Ca2+ suppresses polymerization elsewhere in the lamella and lamellipod is also unknown, although Ca2+-sensitive capping proteins expressed in T cells such as gelsolin (Yin, 1987) or CapG (Yu et al., 1990) are attractive candidates.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms, based on known Ca2+-sensitive proteins.

claim: Ca2+-dependent acceleration of depolymerization is unlikely to involve myosin.
source: Our results indicate that Ca2+-dependent acceleration of depolymerization is unlikely to involve myosin (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B), but the actin-severing proteins cofilin (Maus et al., 2013; Meberg et al., 1998; Wang et al., 2005) and gelsolin (Yin, 1987) remain viable candidates as both are expressed in T cells and respond to physiological levels of [Ca2+]i (Lin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the blebbistatin experiments, with speculation about alternative mechanisms.

claim: The location and dynamics of the ER are critical factors that determine when and where Ca2+ influx sites arise when T cells contact their targets.
source: Because the ER-PM junction forms the physical site for STIM1-Orai1 assembly into active CRAC channels, the location and dynamics of the ER are critical factors that determine when and where Ca2+ influx sites arise when T cells contact their targets.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the known role of ER-PM junctions in CRAC channel function.

claim: The first mechanism for STIM1 and Orai1 appearance in the cSMAC/ADZ is related to the movement of the centrosome and associated MTOC to the synapse.
source: The first is related to the movement of the centrosome and associated MTOC to the synapse, as EM tomography has shown enrichment of the ER around the centrosome at synaptic contact sites (Ueda et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on prior literature about ER localization around the centrosome.

claim: Nascent ER tubules may form ER-PM junctions in peripheral regions, which then enable the assembly of active STIM1-Orai1 complexes that traverse the lamella before they are collected in the ADZ.
source: Our observations that STIM1/Orai1 puncta and actin move towards the ADZ at similar speeds suggest that nascent ER tubules may form ER-PM junctions in peripheral regions, which then enable the assembly of active STIM1-Orai1 complexes that traverse the lamella before they are collected in the ADZ.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed similar velocities of STIM1/Orai1 puncta and actin.

claim: Intracellular Ca2+ binding to membrane phospholipids is thought to enhance TCR signaling by exposing membrane-associated CD3 ITAM motifs.
source: Interestingly, intracellular Ca2+ binding to membrane phospholipids is thought to enhance TCR signaling by exposing membrane-associated CD3 ITAM motifs (Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited reference.

claim: Mobile CRAC channel complexes may create local sites of high [Ca2+]i needed to fully activate mobile TCR microclusters.
source: Thus, an intriguing possibility is that mobile CRAC channel complexes create local sites of high [Ca2+]i needed to fully activate mobile TCR microclusters.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed mobility of CRAC channels and the known effects of Ca2+ on TCR signaling.

claim: The action of Ca2+ influx to promote actin turnover and flow creates a positive feedback loop that would be expected to maintain or enhance the activation of CRAC channels.
source: Because actin dynamics are required to sustain TCR activity at the synapse (Kaizuka et al., 2007; Valitutti et al., 1995; Varma et al., 2006; Rivas et al., 2004; Babich et al., 2012; Yi et al., 2012; Kumari et al., 2015), the action of Ca2+ influx to promote actin turnover and flow creates a positive feedback loop that would be expected to maintain or enhance the activation of CRAC channels.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed effects of Ca2+ on actin and the known role of actin in TCR signaling.

claim: This positive feedback loop creates the potential for nonlinear effects, such that graded increases or decreases in [Ca2+]i may act through actin to modulate TCR activity and bias the cell towards all-or-none, threshold-like behavior in response to antigen.
source: This loop creates the potential for nonlinear effects, such that graded increases or decreases in [Ca2+]i may act through actin to modulate TCR activity and bias the cell towards all-or-none, threshold-like behavior in response to antigen.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional consequences of the observed Ca2+-actin feedback loop.

claim: Ca2+ influx effectively limits the lifetime of active TCR microclusters by increasing the rate at which they are transported to the synapse center, where signaling is terminated.
source: At the same time, Ca2+ influx effectively limits the lifetime of active TCR microclusters by increasing the rate at which they are transported to the synapse center, where signaling is terminated (Yu et al., 2010; Varma et al., 2006; Yokosuka et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed effects of Ca2+ on actin flow and the known role of actin flow in TCR microcluster transport.

claim: The accumulation of STIM1 and Orai1 in the ADZ reveals a new type of CRAC channel self-organization.
source: In addition, the accumulation of STIM1 and Orai1 in the ADZ reveals a new type of CRAC channel self-organization.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed STIM1/Orai1 localization patterns.

claim: At the level of single ER-PM junctions, STIM1 and Orai1 complexes self-organize through a diffusion trap mechanism based on STIM1 binding to the PM and Orai1.
source: At the level of single ER-PM junctions, STIM1 and Orai1 complexes self-organize through a diffusion trap mechanism based on STIM1 binding to the PM and Orai1 (Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited reference.

claim: At the synapse, CRAC channels self-organize in a second way, by promoting the retrograde flow of actin that concentrates ER-PM junctions and CRAC channels in the ADZ.
source: At the synapse CRAC channels self-organize in a second way, by promoting the retrograde flow of actin that concentrates ER-PM junctions and CRAC channels in the ADZ.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed effects of Ca2+ on actin flow and ER/CRAC channel localization.

claim: CRAC channel self-organization may ensure that Ca2+ is optimally positioned to serve critical Ca2+-dependent functions including the directional secretion of cytokines.
source: Given evidence that Ca2+ locally regulates exocytosis in T cells and mast cells (Pores-Fernando and Zweifach, 2009; Holowka et al., 2012) CRAC channel self-organization may ensure that Ca2+ is optimally positioned to serve critical Ca2+-dependent functions including the directional secretion of cytokines like interleukin 2 and interferon-γ (Huse et al., 2006) that drive subsequent phases of the immune response.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of CRAC channel localization, based on prior literature.
